title: Letter Case Permutation
description: Given a string s containing lowercase letters and digits, return every string that can be formed by toggling the case of any subset of the letters. Digits stay unchanged. Return the permutations in lexicographic order (uppercase letters sort before lowercase).

examples.explanation: Each of the 2 letters can be upper or lower case; results are sorted lexicographically.
Only the letter z branches into two cases.

constraints: s consists of lowercase English letters and digits.
hints: Each letter doubles the number of results, while digits are fixed.
Build the answer character by character, branching into two cases only when you see a letter.

title: Binary Watch
description: A binary watch has 4 LEDs for the hour (8, 4, 2, 1) and 6 LEDs for the minute (32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1). Given turnedOn, the number of LEDs that are lit, return every possible time as a string "h:mm" (no leading zero on the hour, e.g. "1:00"), in lexicographic order.

examples.explanation: One lit LED gives the 10 times above, sorted lexicographically.
No valid hour/minute pair lights exactly 9 LEDs.

hints: Try every hour from 0 to 11 and every minute from 0 to 59.
A time is valid when the number of set bits in the hour plus the number of set bits in the minute equals turnedOn.

title: All Paths From Source to Target
description: Given a directed acyclic graph with n nodes labeled 0 to n-1 as an adjacency list graph, return every path from node 0 to node n-1, in lexicographic order.

examples.explanation: The only path goes straight from 0 to 1.
All five routes from 0 to 4, sorted lexicographically.

constraints: There is at least one path from node 0 to node n-1.
hints: Do a depth-first walk starting at node 0, extending the current path.
When you reach node n-1, record a copy of the current path, then backtrack.

title: Generate Binary Strings Without Adjacent Zeros
description: Given an integer n, return every binary string of length n that contains no two adjacent 0s, in lexicographic order.

examples.explanation: "000", "001" and "100" are excluded for having adjacent zeros.
Both single characters are valid.

hints: Build the string one character at a time.
You may always append 1; you may append 0 only when the previous character is not 0.

title: Sum of All Subset XOR Totals
description: The XOR total of an array is the XOR of all its elements, or 0 for the empty array. Given an array nums, return the sum of the XOR totals of all 2^n subsets.

examples.explanation: The subset XORs are 0, 1, 3, 2, summing to 6.
The eight subset XOR totals sum to 28.

hints: Enumerate every subset and accumulate its XOR.
For each element, decide include or skip while carrying the running XOR.

title: Generate All Binary Strings
description: Given an integer n, return all 2^n binary strings of length n, in lexicographic order.

examples.explanation: All four 2-bit strings, sorted lexicographically.
The two 1-bit strings.

hints: Each position independently chooses 0 or 1.
Recurse position by position, trying 0 before 1 to get lexicographic order.

title: Count Valid Parenthesis Combinations
description: Given n pairs of parentheses, return how many distinct strings of length 2n form valid (well-balanced) parentheses.

examples.explanation: Only "()".

hints: Track how many opening and closing brackets you have placed so far.
You may always place "(" while opens < n, and place ")" only while closes < opens.

title: Binary Tree Paths
description: Given the root of a binary tree, return all root-to-leaf paths, each formatted as node values joined by "->". Visit the left subtree before the right subtree.

examples.explanation: Leaves are 5 and 3; the left path comes first.
The single node is itself a root-to-leaf path.

hints: Walk down from the root, appending each node value to the current path.
When you reach a leaf (no children), record the joined path, then backtrack.

title: Subsets
description: Given an integer array nums of unique elements, return all possible subsets (the power set). Return the subsets in lexicographic order (compare element by element; shorter prefix first).

examples.explanation: All 2^3 subsets, sorted lexicographically.
All 2^2 subsets, sorted lexicographically.

constraints: All elements of nums are unique.
hints: Decide for each element, in order, whether to include it.
A recursive include/skip choice naturally enumerates every subset once.

title: Permutations
description: Given an array nums of distinct integers, return all possible permutations, in lexicographic order.

examples.explanation: All 6 permutations, sorted lexicographically.
A single element has one permutation.

constraints: All integers of nums are unique.
hints: Build each permutation one position at a time, picking any unused element.
A boolean "used" array tracks which elements are already placed.

title: Combination Sum
description: Given an array of distinct integers candidates and a target, return every unique combination of candidates that sums to target. Each candidate may be used an unlimited number of times. Write each combination in ascending order, and return the combinations in lexicographic order.

examples.explanation: 2+2+3 and 7 both sum to 7.
All combinations summing to 8, each sorted ascending.

constraints: All elements of candidates are distinct.
hints: Sort candidates first so each combination is built in ascending order.
At each step, either reuse the current candidate or move to the next one; stop when the remaining target hits 0 or goes negative.

title: Generate Parentheses
description: Given n pairs of parentheses, return all strings of n pairs that form valid parentheses, in lexicographic order.

examples.explanation: All 5 valid arrangements, sorted lexicographically.
Only one arrangement.

hints: Track how many opening and closing brackets are placed.
Place "(" while opens < n; place ")" while closes < opens.

title: Letter Combinations of a Phone Number
description: Given a string digits containing digits 2-9, return every letter combination the digits could represent (telephone keypad: 2=abc, 3=def, 4=ghi, 5=jkl, 6=mno, 7=pqrs, 8=tuv, 9=wxyz), in lexicographic order. An empty input returns an empty list.

examples.output: [ad, ae, af, bd, be, bf, cd, ce, cf]
examples.explanation: 3 x 3 combinations, already in lexicographic order.
The three letters on key 2.

constraints: digits[i] is a digit in the range 2-9.

sampleTests.expected: [ad, ae, af, bd, be, bf, cd, ce, cf]

hiddenTests.expected: [pw, px, py, pz, qw, qx, qy, qz, rw, rx, ry, rz, sw, sx, sy, sz]
[adg, adh, adi, aeg, aeh, aei, afg, afh, afi, bdg, bdh, bdi, beg, beh, bei, bfg, bfh, bfi, cdg, cdh, cdi, ceg, ceh, cei, cfg, cfh, cfi]
[aa, ab, ac, ba, bb, bc, ca, cb, cc]

hints: Map each digit to its letters, then pick one letter per digit position.
Recurse digit by digit; each digit branches over its 3-4 letters.

title: Palindrome Partitioning
description: Given a string s, return every partition of s such that every substring is a palindrome, in lexicographic order. Return each partition as a single string with its parts joined by '|' (e.g. "a|a|b"). List the partitions in lexicographic order of these encoded strings.

examples.explanation: "aab" splits into single letters or "aa"+"b".
Both the all-single split and the whole palindrome.

constraints: s contains only lowercase English letters.
hints: Try every possible end position for the first substring.
Only continue down a branch when the chosen prefix is a palindrome.

title: Word Search
description: Given an m x n grid of characters board and a string word, return true if word can be formed by a path of 4-directionally adjacent cells, using each cell at most once.

examples.explanation: No path spells ABCB without reusing cells.

constraints: board and word consist of uppercase English letters.

sampleTests.input:
[[A, B, C, E], [S, F, C, S], [A, D, E, E]]
ABCCED

[[A, B, C, E], [S, F, C, S], [A, D, E, E]]
ABCB

hiddenTests.input:
[[A, B, C, E], [S, F, C, S], [A, D, E, E]]
SEE

[[A, B, C, E], [S, F, C, S], [A, D, E, E]]
ABCE

[[A, B, C, E], [S, F, C, S], [A, D, E, E]]
SFCS

[[A, B, C, E], [S, F, C, S], [A, D, E, E]]
ABCCEDX

hints: Start a depth-first search from every cell matching the first letter.
Mark a cell visited while exploring from it and unmark it when backtracking.

title: Restore IP Addresses
description: Given a string s of digits, return every valid IPv4 address that can be formed by inserting three dots. A segment is 0-255 with no leading zeros unless the segment is exactly "0". Return the addresses in lexicographic order.

examples.explanation: The two valid splittings, sorted lexicographically.
Each segment must be exactly "0".

hints: Place the three dots by choosing lengths 1-3 for each of the first three segments.
Prune a branch as soon as a segment has a leading zero or exceeds 255.

title: N-Queens
description: Place n queens on an n x n board so no two attack each other. Return every distinct board, each as a list of n strings with "Q" and "." characters. Order the solutions lexicographically by their joined rows. Return each solution as a single string with its rows joined by '|' (e.g. ".Q..|...Q|Q...|..Q."). List the solutions in lexicographic order of these encoded strings.

examples.explanation: The two 4-queen solutions, sorted lexicographically by rows.
One queen on a 1x1 board.

hints: Place queens row by row, one per row.
A new queen is safe when its column and both diagonals are free of earlier queens.

title: Sudoku Solver
description: Solve a Sudoku puzzle. The board is given as 9 strings of 9 characters each, with "." for empty cells. Return the solved board as 9 strings. The puzzle is guaranteed to have exactly one solution.

examples.explanation: The classic puzzle, fully solved.
Another valid puzzle with a unique solution.

constraints: The input board is a valid solvable Sudoku with exactly one solution.
hints: Find an empty cell and try digits 1-9 in it.
Keep row/column/box usage sets so each candidate digit is tested in O(1); undo the placement when backtracking.

title: N-Queens II
description: Count the number of distinct ways to place n queens on an n x n board so no two attack each other.

examples.explanation: The two solutions from the N-Queens problem.
A single queen fits trivially.

hints: This is N-Queens without recording the boards - just count.
Place queens row by row and increment the count when all n rows are filled.

title: Word Search II
description: Given an m x n board of characters and a list of words, return every word that can be formed by a path of 4-directionally adjacent cells without reusing a cell. List each found word at most once, in lexicographic order.

examples.explanation: "oath" and "eat" are found; "pea" and "rain" are not.
"abcb" would need to reuse a cell.

constraints: words[i] consists of lowercase English letters.

sampleTests.input:
[[o, a, a, n], [e, t, a, e], [i, h, k, r], [i, f, l, v]]
["oath", "pea", "eat", "rain"]

hiddenTests.input:
[[a, b, c], [d, e, f], [g, h, i]]
["abc", "cfi", "beh", "aei", "ab"]

[[c, a, t], [r, r, e], [t, o, n]]
["cat", "cater", "ton", "note"]

hints: Searching each word separately with the Word Search DFS is correct; a trie makes it faster.
Collect found words in a set so duplicates in the input list are reported once.
